Improved algebraic lower bound for the radius of spatial analyticity for the generalized KdV equationThanks: This work was partially supported by CAPES, CNPq and FAPESP, Brazil.

Mikaela Baldasso and Mahenda Panthee Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Campinas
13083-859 Campinas, SP, Brazil Email address: mikaelabaldasso@gmail.com, mpanthee@unicamp.br
Abstract.

We consider the initial value problema (IVP) for the generalized Korteweg-de Vries (gKdV) equation

{∂tu+∂x3u+μ​uk​∂xu=0,x∈ℝ,t∈ℝ,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),\displaystyle\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{3}u+\mu u^{k}\partial_{x}u=0,\,&x\in\mathbb{R},\,t\in\mathbb{R},\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\end{cases}

where u⁡(x,t)u(x,\,t) is a real valued function, u0​(x)u_{0}(x) is a real analytic function, μ=±1\mu=\pm 1 and k≥4k\geq 4. We prove that if the initial data u0u_{0} has radius of analyticity σ0\sigma_{0}, than there exists T0>0T_{0}>0 such that the radius of spatial analyticity of the solution remains the same in the time interval [−T0,T0][-T_{0},\,T_{0}]. In the defocusing case, for k≥4k\geq 4 even, we prove that when the local solution extends globally in time, then for any T≥T0T\geq T_{0}, the radius of analyticity cannot decay faster than c​T−(2​kk+4+ϵ)cT^{-\left(\frac{2k}{k+4}+\epsilon\right)}, ϵ>0\epsilon>0 arbitrarily small and c>0c>0 a constant. The result of this work improves the one obtained by Bona et al. in [5].

Keywords: Generalized KdV equation, Cauchy problem, radius of spatial analyticity, Bourgain spaces, Gevrey spaces, almost conserved quantity.

2020 AMS Subject Classification: 35A20, 35B40, 35Q35, 35Q53.

1. Introduction

Consider the initial value problem (IVP) for the generalized Korteweg-de Vries (gKdV) equation:

{∂tu+∂x3u+μ​uk​∂xu=0,x∈ℝ,t∈ℝ,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),\displaystyle\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{3}u+\mu u^{k}\partial_{x}u=0,\,&x\in\mathbb{R},\,t\in\mathbb{R},\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\end{cases} (1.1)

where the unknown u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) and the initial data u0​(x)u_{0}(x) are real-valued, μ=±1\mu=\pm 1 and k≥4k\geq 4. When μ=1\mu=1, the equation (1.1) is known as focusing and defocusing for μ=−1\mu=-1.

It is well-known that the real solution for the IVP (1.1) enjoys the mass conservation

M⁡(u⁡(t))=∫ℝu2​(x,t)​𝑑x=M⁡(u0),M(u(t))=\int_{\mathbb{R}}u^{2}(x,\,t)dx=M(u_{0}), (1.2)

and the energy conservation

E⁡(u⁡(t))=∫ℝ(∂xu)2​(x,t)​𝑑x−2​μ(k+1)​(k+2)​∫ℝuk+2​(x,t)​𝑑x,E(u(t))=\int_{\mathbb{R}}(\partial_{x}u)^{2}(x,\,t)dx-\frac{2\mu}{(k+1)(k+2)}\int_{\mathbb{R}}u^{k+2}(x,\,t)dx, (1.3)

and these quantities will be useful in this work.

Well-posedness issues of the IVP (1.1) for k≥1k\geq 1 with given initial data in the classical Sobolev spaces Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) have been extensively studied by several authors, see [6], [7], [8], [20], [21] and references therein. Particularly, for k=4k=4, Kenig, Ponce and Vega [21] proved the local well-posedness in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s≥0s\geq 0 which yields global solutions for small data. The global well-posedness for given data with Sobolev norm not so small was proved by Fonseca, Linares and Ponce [10] in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}), s>3/4s>3/4. In [7], Farah improved the latter result and lowered the index to s>3/5s>3/5 and posteriorly, the authors in [24] extended the global well-posedness for s>6/13s>6/13. For k≥5k\geq 5, the best local well-posedness known results in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) are for s>12−2ks>\frac{1}{2}-\frac{2}{k}, which attain the critical scaling indices. In the defocusing case (μ=−1\mu=-1) and kk even, Farah, Linares and Pastor, in [8], established the global well-posedness in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s>4​(k−1)5​ks>\frac{4(k-1)}{5k}. For the focusing case (μ=1\mu=1) or the defocusing case (μ=−1\mu=-1) with kk odd, the same authors also proved the global well-posedness in H1​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}) for sufficiently small data.

In this work we are interested in studying the well-posedness of the IVP (1.1) with real analytic initial data u0u_{0}. For this purpose, we consider u0u_{0} in the Gevrey space Gσ,s​(ℝ)G^{\sigma,\,s}(\mathbb{R}), σ>0\sigma>0 and s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, defined as

Gσ,s​(ℝ)={f∈L2​(ℝ):‖f‖Gσ,s​(ℝ)2=∫ℝ⟨ξ⟩2​s​e2​σ​|ξ|​|f^​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ<∞},G^{\sigma,\,s}(\mathbb{R})=\left\{f\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}):\,||f||_{G^{\sigma,\,s}(\mathbb{R})}^{2}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\langle\xi\rangle^{2s}e^{2\sigma|\xi|}|\hat{f}(\xi)|^{2}d\xi<\infty\right\},

where f^\hat{f} denotes the spatial Fourier transform of ff,

f^​(ξ)=12​π​∫ℝe−i​x​ξ​f​(x)​𝑑x.\hat{f}(\xi)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-ix\xi}f(x)dx.

The interest in these spaces is due to the following fact.

Paley-Wiener Theorem.

Let σ>0\sigma>0 and s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}. Then, the following are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    f∈Gσ,sf\in G^{\sigma,\,s}.

  2. (2)

    ff is the restriction to the real line of a function FF which is holomorphic in the strip

    Sσ={x+iy:x,y∈ℝ,|y|<σ}S_{\sigma}=\{x+iy:\,x,\,y\in\mathbb{R},\,|y|<\sigma\}

    and satisfies

    sup|y|<σ‖F⁡(x+i​y)‖Hxs<∞.\sup_{|y|<\sigma}||F(x+iy)||_{H_{x}^{s}}<\infty.

In this sense, σ\sigma is called the uniform radius of analyticity and a natural question concerning this space is: given u0∈Gσ,su_{0}\in G^{\sigma,\,s} is it possible to guarantee the existence of solution such that the radius of analyticity remains the same at least for short time? And after extending the local solution globally in time, how does the radius of analyticity evolve in time? This sort of questions for the dispersive equations are widely studied in the literature, see for example [1], [2], [5], [9], [13], [16], [19], [25], [26], [27] and references therein. Se also [15], [17], [18], [23] and references therein for the problems posed in the periodic domain 𝕋\mathbb{T}.

Concerning the IVP (1.1) for k≥1k\geq 1 with data in the Gevrey spaces Gσ,s​(ℝ)G^{\sigma,\,s}(\mathbb{R}), we mention the work of Bona et al. in [5] where the authors proved the global well-posedness results and obtained algebraic lower bounds for the radius of analyticity as time advances. More precisely, for the KdV (k=1k=1) and the mKdV (k=2k=2) equations, they obtained c​T−12cT^{-12} as an algebraic lower bound for the evolution of the radius of analyticity and c​T−(k2+3​k+2)cT^{-(k^{2}+3k+2)} for k≥3k\geq 3. Recently, in [25], Selberg and Silva introduced the concept of almost conserved quantity and improved the result in [5] obtaining c​T−(43+ϵ)cT^{-(\frac{4}{3}+\epsilon)} as a lower bound for the radius of analyticity for the KdV equation. For the gKdV equation with k=3k=3, Selberg and Tesfahun obtained, in [27], c​T−2cT^{-2} as a lower bound for the radius of spatial analyticity. In both the KdV equation and the gKdV equation with k=3k=3, almost conserved quantities at the L2L^{2}-level of Sobolev regularity are used. For the mKdV equation (k=2)(k=2) no well-posedness result exists at the L2L^{2}-level of Sobolev regularity. This suggests that, if one wishes to use the idea of almost conserved quantity it is necessary to work in the higher level of Sobolev regularity. Quite recently, the second author with Figueira, in [9], constructed almost conserved quantity at the H1H^{1}-level of Sobolev regularity and obtained the lower bound c​T−43cT^{-\frac{4}{3}} for the radius of analyticity to the mKdV equation improving the result in [5]. Now, a natural question that arise is that whether it is possible to construct almost conserved quantity for the gKdV equation with k≥4k\geq 4 so as to improve the lower bound for the radius of analyticity obtained in [5].

In the present work, taking motivation from [9], we will respond the question raised in the previous paragraph affirmatively by constructing almost conserved quantity at the H1H^{1}-level of Sobolev regularity (see (4.22) and (4.26) below) and improve significantly the result in [5] for the defocusing gKdV equation (1.1) with k≥4k\geq 4 even.

Regarding the local well-posedness, we first prove the following result that is valid for both focusing and defocusing cases and for every integer k≥4k\geq 4.

Theorem 1.1.

Let σ>0\sigma>0, k≥4k\geq 4 and s>k−42​ks>\frac{k-4}{2k}. For given u0∈Gσ,s​(ℝ)u_{0}\in G^{\sigma,\,s}(\mathbb{R}), there exists T0=T0​(‖u0‖Gσ,s)>0T_{0}=T_{0}(||u_{0}||_{G^{\sigma,\,s}})>0 such that the IVP (1.1) admits a unique solution u∈C⁡([−T0,T0],Gσ,s​(ℝ))u\in C([-T_{0},\,T_{0}];G^{\sigma,\,s}(\mathbb{R})). Moreover, the data-to-solution map is locally Lipschitz.

Thus, for short time, the solution remains analytic in the same initial strip. Our main result concerning the global well-posedness and the evolution of the radius of analyticity is the following.

Theorem 1.2.

Let σ0>0\sigma_{0}>0, k≥4k\geq 4 even, s>k−42​ks>\frac{k-4}{2k}, u0∈Gσ,s​(ℝ)u_{0}\in G^{\sigma,\,s}(\mathbb{R}) and uu be the local solution to the IVP (1.1) in the defocusing case (μ=−1\mu=-1) given by Theorem 1.1. Then, for any T≥T0T\geq T_{0}, the local solution uu extends globally in time satisfying

u∈C⁡([−T,T],Gσ⁡(T),s​(ℝ)),with ​σ​(T)≥min⁡{σ0,c​T−(2​kk+4+ϵ)},u\in C([-T,\,T];G^{\sigma(T),\,s}(\mathbb{R})),\quad\text{with }\sigma(T)\geq\min\left\{\sigma_{0},\,cT^{-\left(\frac{2k}{k+4}+\epsilon\right)}\right\},

where ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is arbitrarily small and cc is a positive constant depending on kk, ss, σ0\sigma_{0} and ‖u0‖Gσ,s||u_{0}||_{G^{\sigma,\,s}}.

To prove Theorem 1.2, we derive an almost conserved quantity in Gσ, 1​(ℝ)G^{\sigma,\,1}(\mathbb{R}) space using the conserved quantities (1.2) and (1.3). Once having the almost conserved quantity at hand, we are able to prove the global result by decomposing any interval of time [0,T][0,\,T] into short subintervals and iterate the local result in each subinterval. During this iteration process there appears a restriction that gives the lower bound for σ⁡(T)\sigma(T).

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we define the Bourgain’s spaces and record some preliminary estimates. The proof of the local well-posedness result stated in Theorem 1.1 is contained in Section 3. In Section 4 we derive the almost conserved quantity and find the associated decay estimates. Finally, in Section 5 we extend the local solution globally in time and obtain an algebraic lower bound for the radius of analyticity stated in Theorem 1.2.

2. Function Spaces and k-linear estimates

In this section we discuss the function spaces that will be used throughout this work and derive some k-linear estimates that play crucial role in the proofs.

First, regarding the Gevrey space defined in Section 1, we have the embedding

Gσ,s⊂Gσ′,s′for all ​0<σ′<σ​ and ​s,s′∈ℝ,G^{\sigma,\,s}\subset G^{\sigma^{\prime},\,s^{\prime}}\quad\text{for all }0<\sigma^{\prime}<\sigma\text{ and }s,\,s^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}, (2.1)

and the inclusion is continuous in the sense that there exists a constant C>0C>0 depending on σ,σ′,s,s′\sigma,\,\sigma^{\prime},\,s,\,s^{\prime} such that

‖f‖Gσ′,s′≤C​‖f‖Gσ,s.||f||_{G^{\sigma^{\prime},\,s^{\prime}}}\leq C||f||_{G^{\sigma,\,s}}.

In addition to the Gevrey space, we use a space that is a mix between the Gevrey space and the Bourgain’s space introduced in [3] and [4]. Given σ≥0\sigma\geq 0 and s,b∈ℝs,\,b\in\mathbb{R}, we define the Gevrey-Bourgain space, denoted by Xσ,s,b​(ℝ2)X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), as the closure of the Schwartz space under the norm

‖u‖Xσ,s,b=‖eσ​|ξ|​⟨ξ⟩s​⟨τ−ξ3⟩b​u~​(ξ,τ)‖Lτ,ξ2,||u||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}=||e^{\sigma|\xi|}\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\langle\tau-\xi^{3}\rangle^{b}\tilde{u}(\xi,\tau)||_{L^{2}_{\tau,\,\xi}},

where ⟨ξ⟩=1+|ξ|\langle\xi\rangle=1+|\xi| and u~\tilde{u} denotes the space-time Fourier transform of uu. For σ=0\sigma=0, we recover the classical Bourgain’s space Xs,b​(ℝ2)X^{s,\,b}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) with the norm given by

‖u‖Xs,b=‖⟨ξ⟩s​⟨τ−ξ3⟩b​u~​(ξ,τ)‖Lτ,ξ2.||u||_{X^{s,\,b}}=||\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\langle\tau-\xi^{3}\rangle^{b}\tilde{u}(\xi,\tau)||_{L^{2}_{\tau,\,\xi}}.

For T>0T>0 the restrictions of Xs,b​(ℝ2)X^{s,\,b}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) and Xσ,s,b​(ℝ2)X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) to a time slab ℝ×(−T,T)\mathbb{R}\times(-T,\,T), denoted by XTs,b​(ℝ2)X_{T}^{s,\,b}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) and XTσ,s,b​(ℝ2)X_{T}^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), respectively, are Banach spaces when equipped with the norms

‖u‖XTs,b\displaystyle||u||_{X_{T}^{s,\,b}} =inf​{‖v‖Xs,b:v=u​ on ​ℝ×(−T,T)},\displaystyle=\text{inf}\{||v||_{X^{s,\,b}}:v=u\text{ on }\mathbb{R}\times(-T,\,T)\},
‖u‖XTσ,s,b\displaystyle||u||_{X_{T}^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}} =inf​{‖v‖Xσ,s,b:v=u​ on ​ℝ×(−T,T)}.\displaystyle=\text{inf}\{||v||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}:v=u\text{ on }\mathbb{R}\times(-T,\,T)\}.

To simplify the exposition we introduce the operator eσ​|Dx|e^{\sigma|D_{x}|} given by

eσ​|Dx|​u^​(ξ)=eσ​|ξ|​u^​(ξ)\widehat{e^{\sigma|D_{x}|}u}(\xi)=e^{\sigma|\xi|}\hat{u}(\xi)

so that, one has

‖eσ​|Dx|​u‖Xs,b=‖u‖Xσ,s,b.||e^{\sigma|D_{x}|}u||_{X^{s,\,b}}=||u||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}. (2.2)

Substituting uu by eσ​|Dx|​ue^{\sigma|D_{x}|}u, the relation (2.2) allows us to carry out the properties of Xs,bX^{s,\,b} and XTs,bX_{T}^{s,\,b} spaces over Xσ,s,bX^{\sigma,\,s,\,b} and XTσ,s,bX_{T}^{\sigma,\,s,\,b} spaces.

In the case σ=0\sigma=0, for the proof of the first lemma below we refer to Section 2.6 of [28] and the second lemma follows by the argument used to prove Lemma 7 in [26]. The proofs for σ>0\sigma>0 follow analogously using the relation (2.2).

Let σ≥0\sigma\geq 0, s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R} and b>12b>\frac{1}{2}. Then, Xσ,s,b​(ℝ2)⊂C⁡(ℝ,Gσ,s)X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\subset C(\mathbb{R},\,G^{\sigma,\,s}) and

3. Local well-posedness - Proof of Theorem 1.1

In this section we use the estimates from the previous section and provide a proof for the local well-posedness result to the IVP (1.1) for given real analytic initial data.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Let σ>0\sigma>0, u0∈Gσ,s​(ℝ)u_{0}\in G^{\sigma,\,s}(\mathbb{R}) with s>k−42​ks>\frac{k-4}{2k}. For 0<T≤10<T\leq 1, let ψT\psi_{T} be the cut-off function as defined earlier and consider a solution map given by

ΦT​(u)=ψ⁡(t)​W​(t)​u0−ψT​(t)​∫0tW⁡(t−t′)​μ5​∂x(uk+1)​d​t′.\Phi_{T}(u)=\psi(t)W(t)u_{0}-\psi_{T}(t)\int_{0}^{t}W(t-t^{\prime})\frac{\mu}{5}\partial_{x}(u^{k+1})dt^{\prime}.

Our main goal is to show that there are b>12b>\frac{1}{2}, r>0r>0 and T0=T0​(‖u0‖Gσ,s)T_{0}=T_{0}(||u_{0}||_{G^{\sigma,\,s}}) such that ΦT0:B⁡(r)→B⁡(r)\Phi_{T_{0}}:B(r)\rightarrow B(r) is a contraction map, where

B⁡(r)={u∈XT0σ,s,b:‖u‖Xσ,s,b≤r}.B(r)=\left\{u\in X_{T_{0}}^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}:||u||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}\leq r\right\}.

For u∈B⁡(r)u\in B(r), applying the linear inequalities (2.4) and (2.5) and the estimate (2.7) with b=12+ϵb=\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon and b′=12+2​ϵb^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2}+2\epsilon as in the Proposition 2.5, we obtain

‖ΦT​(u)‖Xσ,s,b≤‖ψ⁡(t)​W​(t)​u0‖Xσ,s,b+||ψT​(t)​∫0tW⁡(t−t′)​μ5​∂x(uk+1)​d​t′||Xσ,s,b≤C​‖u0‖Gσ,s+C​T1a​‖∂x(uk+1)‖Xσ,s,b′−1≤C​‖u0‖Gσ,s+C​T1a​‖u‖Xσ,s,bk+1≤r2+C​T1a​rk+1,\begin{split}||\Phi_{T}(u)||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}&\leq||\psi(t)W(t)u_{0}||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}+\left|\left|\psi_{T}(t)\int_{0}^{t}W(t-t^{\prime})\frac{\mu}{5}\partial_{x}(u^{k+1})dt^{\prime}\right|\right|_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}\\ &\leq C||u_{0}||_{G^{\sigma,\,s}}+CT^{\frac{1}{a}}||\partial_{x}(u^{k+1})||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b^{\prime}-1}}\\ &\leq C||u_{0}||_{G^{\sigma,\,s}}+CT^{\frac{1}{a}}||u||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}^{k+1}\\ &\leq\frac{r}{2}+CT^{\frac{1}{a}}r^{k+1},\end{split} (3.1)

where 1a=b′−b\frac{1}{a}=b^{\prime}-b and r=2​C​‖u0‖Gσ,sr=2C||u_{0}||_{G^{\sigma,\,s}}.

By choosing

T0≤1(2​C​rk)a,T_{0}\leq\frac{1}{(2Cr^{k})^{a}}, (3.2)

one gets from (3.1) that ‖ΦT0​(u)‖Xσ,s,b≤r||\Phi_{T_{0}}(u)||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}\leq r for all u∈B⁡(r)u\in B(r) showing that ΦT0​(B⁡(r))⊂B⁡(r)\Phi_{T_{0}}(B(r))\subset B(r).

Now, for uu, v∈B⁡(r)v\in B(r), using (2.5) once again, we have

‖ΦT0​(u)−ΦT0​(v)‖Xσ,s,b≤C​T01a​‖∂x(uk+1)−∂x(vk+1)‖Xσ,s,b′.||\Phi_{T_{0}}(u)-\Phi_{T_{0}}(v)||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}\leq CT_{0}^{\frac{1}{a}}||\partial_{x}(u^{k+1})-\partial_{x}(v^{k+1})||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b^{\prime}}}.

Since

uk+1−vk+1=(u−v)​∑i=0kui​vk−i,u^{k+1}-v^{k+1}=(u-v)\sum_{i=0}^{k}u^{i}v^{k-i},

from (2.6) we conclude that

‖ΦT0​(u)−ΦT0​(v)‖Xσ,s,b≤C​T01a​||∂x((u−v)​∑i=0kui​vk−i)||Xσ,s,b′≤C​T01a||u−v|​|∑i=0kXσ,s,b⁡‖u‖Xσ,s,bi|​|v||Xσ,s,bk−i≤C​T01a​(k+1)​rk​‖u−v‖Xσ,s,b\begin{split}||\Phi_{T_{0}}(u)-\Phi_{T_{0}}(v)||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}&\leq CT_{0}^{\frac{1}{a}}\left|\left|\partial_{x}\left((u-v)\sum_{i=0}^{k}u^{i}v^{k-i}\right)\right|\right|_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b^{\prime}}}\\ &\leq CT_{0}^{\frac{1}{a}}||u-v||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}\sum_{i=0}^{k}||u||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}^{i}||v||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}^{k-i}\\ &\leq CT_{0}^{\frac{1}{a}}(k+1)r^{k}||u-v||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}\end{split} (3.3)

By choosing

T0≤1(2​C​(k+1)​rk)a,T_{0}\leq\frac{1}{(2C(k+1)r^{k})^{a}}, (3.4)

it follows from (3.3) that

‖ΦT0​(u)−ΦT0​(v)‖Xσ,s,b≤12​‖u−v‖Xσ,s,b||\Phi_{T_{0}}(u)-\Phi_{T_{0}}(v)||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}\leq\frac{1}{2}||u-v||_{X^{\sigma,\,s,\,b}}

and ΦT0\Phi_{T_{0}} is a contraction map.

Finally, it is sufficient to choose 0<T0≤10<T_{0}\leq 1 satisfying (3.2) and (3.4). More precisely, considering

T0=c0(1+‖u0‖Gσ,s2)k2​aT_{0}=\frac{c_{0}}{(1+||u_{0}||_{G^{\sigma,\,s}}^{2})^{\frac{k}{2}a}} (3.5)

The continuous dependence on the initial data follows by a similar argument and the proof is complete. ∎

4. Almost conserved quantity

In order to apply the local result repeatedly to cover arbitrary time interval [−T,T][-T,\,T], for any T>0T>0, we will introduce almost conserved quantity associated to the gKdV equation (1.1) and find some estimates for it. Taking in consideration the conserved quantities (1.2) and (1.3), we define

Eσ​(t)=∫(eσ​|Dx|​u)2​𝑑x+∫(∂x(eσ​|Dx|​u))2​𝑑x−2​μ(k+1)​(k+2)​∫(eσ​|Dx|​u)k+2​𝑑x.E_{\sigma}(t)=\int(e^{\sigma|D_{x}|}u)^{2}dx+\int(\partial_{x}(e^{\sigma|D_{x}|}u))^{2}dx-\frac{2\mu}{(k+1)(k+2)}\int(e^{\sigma|D_{x}|}u)^{k+2}dx. (4.1)

Note that, for σ=0\sigma=0, (4.1) turns out to be the conserved quantities (1.2) and (1.3). However, for σ>0\sigma>0 this fails to hold and our idea is to find a decay estimate for Eσ​(t)E_{\sigma}(t). For this purpose, let U=eσ​|Dx|​uU=e^{\sigma|D_{x}|}u and start by differentiating Eσ​(t)E_{\sigma}(t) with respect to tt, to obtain

dd​t​(Eσ​(t))=2​∫U​Ut​𝑑x+2​∫∂xU​∂x(∂tU)​𝑑x−2​μk+1​∫Uk+1​∂tU​𝑑x.\frac{d}{dt}(E_{\sigma}(t))=2\int UU_{t}dx+2\int\partial_{x}U\partial_{x}(\partial_{t}U)dx-\frac{2\mu}{k+1}\int U^{k+1}\partial_{t}Udx. (4.2)

Applying the operator eσ​|Dx|e^{\sigma|D_{x}|} to the gKdV equation (1.1) equation, we get

∂tU+∂x3U+μ​Uk​∂xU=F⁡(U),\partial_{t}U+\partial_{x}^{3}U+\mu U^{k}\partial_{x}U=F(U), (4.3)

where F⁡(U)F(U) is given by

F⁡(U)=μk+1​∂x[Uk+1−eσ​|Dx|​((e−σ​|Dx|​U)k+1)].F(U)=\frac{\mu}{k+1}\partial_{x}\left[U^{k+1}-e^{\sigma|D_{x}|}\big((e^{-\sigma|D_{x}|}U)^{k+1}\big)\right]. (4.4)

Using (4.3) in each term of (4.2), one has

∫U​∂tU​𝑑x=−∫U∂x3Udx−μk+2∂x(Uk+2)dx+∫UF(U)dx,∫∂xU​∂x(∂tU)​𝑑x=−∫∂xU∂x4Udx−μ∫∂xU∂x(Uk∂xU)dx+∫∂xU∂x(F(U))dx,∫Uk+1​∂tU​𝑑x=−∫Uk+1∂x3Udx−μ∫Uk+1∂xUdx+∫Uk+1F(U)dx.\begin{split}\int U\partial_{t}Udx&=-\int U\partial_{x}^{3}Udx-\frac{\mu}{k+2}\partial_{x}(U^{k+2})dx+\int UF(U)dx,\\ \int\partial_{x}U\partial_{x}(\partial_{t}U)dx&=-\int\partial_{x}U\partial_{x}^{4}Udx-\mu\int\partial_{x}U\partial_{x}(U^{k}\partial_{x}U)dx+\int\partial_{x}U\partial_{x}(F(U))dx,\\ \int U^{k+1}\partial_{t}Udx&=-\int U^{k+1}\partial_{x}^{3}Udx-\mu\int U^{k+1}\partial_{x}Udx+\int U^{k+1}F(U)dx.\end{split}

We can assume that UU and all its partial derivatives tend to zero as |x|→∞|x|\rightarrow\infty (see [25] for a detailed argument) and it follows from integration by parts that

∫U​∂tU​𝑑x\displaystyle\int U\partial_{t}Udx =∫U​F​(U)​𝑑x,\displaystyle=\int UF(U)dx, (4.5)
∫∂xU​∂x(∂tU)​𝑑x\displaystyle\int\partial_{x}U\partial_{x}(\partial_{t}U)dx =−μk+1∫Uk+1∂x3Udx+∫∂xU∂x(F(U))dx,\displaystyle=-\frac{\mu}{k+1}\int U^{k+1}\partial_{x}^{3}Udx+\int\partial_{x}U\partial_{x}(F(U))dx, (4.6)
∫Uk+1​∂tU​𝑑x\displaystyle\int U^{k+1}\partial_{t}Udx =−∫Uk+1∂x3Udx+∫Uk+1F(U)dx.\displaystyle=-\int U^{k+1}\partial_{x}^{3}Udx+\int U^{k+1}F(U)dx. (4.7)

Now, inserting (4.5), (4.6) and (4.7) in (4.2), we get

dd​t​Eσ​(t)=2​∫U​F​(U)​𝑑x+2​∫∂xU​∂x(F⁡(U))​𝑑x−2​μk+1​∫Uk+1​F​(U)​𝑑x.\frac{d}{dt}E_{\sigma}(t)=2\int UF(U)dx+2\int\partial_{x}U\partial_{x}(F(U))dx-\frac{2\mu}{k+1}\int U^{k+1}F(U)dx. (4.8)

Integrating (4.8) in time over [0,t′][0,t^{\prime}] for 0<t′≤T0<t^{\prime}\leq T, we obtain

Eσ​(t′)=Eσ​(0)+Rσ​(t′),E_{\sigma}(t^{\prime})=E_{\sigma}(0)+R_{\sigma}(t^{\prime}), (4.9)

where

Rσ​(t′)=  2​∫∫χ[0,t′]​U​F​(U)​dx​dt+2​∫∫χ[0,t′]​∂xU​∂x(F⁡(U))​dx​dt−−2​μk+1∫∫χ[0,t′]Uk+1F(U)dxdt.\begin{split}R_{\sigma}(t^{\prime})=&\,\,2\int\int\chi_{[0,\,t^{\prime}]}UF(U)dxdt+2\int\int\chi_{[0,\,t^{\prime}]}\partial_{x}U\partial_{x}(F(U))dxdt\,\,-\\ &-\frac{2\mu}{k+1}\int\int\chi_{[0,\,t^{\prime}]}U^{k+1}F(U)dxdt.\end{split} (4.10)

In sequel, we find estimates for F⁡(U)F(U) in the Bourgain’s space norm.

Lemma 4.1.

Let FF be as defined in (4.4) and σ>0\sigma>0. Then, for any b=12+ϵb=\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon, 0<ϵ≪10<\epsilon\ll 1, and for all α∈[0,k+42​k)\alpha\in\left[0,\frac{k+4}{2k}\right),

‖F⁡(U)‖Lx2​Lt2≤C​σα​‖U‖X1,bk+1,||F(U)||_{L_{x}^{2}L_{t}^{2}}\leq C\sigma^{\alpha}||U||_{X^{1,\,b}}^{k+1}, (4.11)
‖∂x(F⁡(U))‖X0,b−1≤C​σα​‖U‖X1,bk+1||\partial_{x}(F(U))||_{X^{0,\,b-1}}\leq C\sigma^{\alpha}||U||_{X^{1,\,b}}^{k+1} (4.12)

for some constant C>0C>0 independent on σ\sigma.

Proof.

Observe that

|F⁡(U)^​(ξ,τ)|≤C​|ξ|​∫∗(1−e−σ⁡(|ξ1|+⋯+|ξk+1|−|ξ|))​|U^​(ξ1,τ1)​|⋯|​U^​(ξk+1,τk+1)|,|\widehat{F(U)}(\xi,\tau)|\leq C|\xi|\int_{*}\big(1-e^{-\sigma(|\xi_{1}|+\cdots+|\xi_{k+1}|-|\xi|)}\big)|\widehat{U}(\xi_{1},\tau_{1})|\cdots|\widehat{U}(\xi_{k+1},\tau_{k+1})|, (4.13)

where ∗* denotes the integral over the set ξ=ξ1+⋯+ξk+1\xi=\xi_{1}+\cdots+\xi_{k+1} and τ=τ1+⋯+τk+1\tau=\tau_{1}+\cdots+\tau_{k+1}.

Now, from the inequality

ex−1≤xα​ex,∀x≥0​ and ​α∈[0, 1],e^{x}-1\leq x^{\alpha}e^{x},\quad\forall\,x\geq 0\text{ and }\alpha\in[0,\,1],

we get

1−e−σ⁡(|ξ1|+⋯+|ξk+1|−|ξ|)≤σα​(|ξ1|+⋯+|ξk+1|−|ξ|)α.1-e^{-\sigma(|\xi_{1}|+\cdots+|\xi_{k+1}|-|\xi|)}\leq\sigma^{\alpha}(|\xi_{1}|+\cdots+|\xi_{k+1}|-|\xi|)^{\alpha}. (4.14)

Without loss of generality, we can assume that |ξ1|≤⋯≤|ξk+1||\xi_{1}|\leq\cdots\leq|\xi_{k+1}|. A simple calculation shows

|ξ1|+⋯+|ξk+1|−|ξ|≤2​k​|ξk|,|\xi_{1}|+\cdots+|\xi_{k+1}|-|\xi|\leq 2k|\xi_{k}|,

and consequently, the estimate (4.14) yields

1−e−σ⁡(|ξ1|+⋯+|ξk+1|−|ξ|)≤C​σα​|ξk|α.1-e^{-\sigma(|\xi_{1}|+\cdots+|\xi_{k+1}|-|\xi|)}\leq C\sigma^{\alpha}|\xi_{k}|^{\alpha}. (4.15)

Using (4.15) in (4.13), we have

|F⁡(U)^​(ξ,τ)|≤C​σα​|ξ|​∫∗|ξk|α​|U^​(ξ1,τ1)​|⋯|​U^​(ξk+1,τk+1)|.|\widehat{F(U)}(\xi,\tau)|\leq C\sigma^{\alpha}|\xi|\int_{*}|\xi_{k}|^{\alpha}|\widehat{U}(\xi_{1},\tau_{1})|\cdots|\widehat{U}(\xi_{k+1},\tau_{k+1})|. (4.16)

Moreover, one has

|ξ|​|ξk|α≤(k+1)​|ξk+1|​|ξk|α.|\xi||\xi_{k}|^{\alpha}\leq(k+1)|\xi_{k+1}||\xi_{k}|^{\alpha}. (4.17)

Now, using (4.17) in (4.16) and an use of Plancherel’s identity implies that

‖F⁡(U)‖Lx2​Lt2≤C​σα​||∫∗|U^​(ξ1,τ1)​|⋯|​U^​(ξk−1,τk−1)​‖Dxα​U^​(ξk,τk)‖​Dx​U^​(ξk+1,τk+1)|||Lξ2​Lτ2=Cσα||w1⋯wk+1||Lx2​Lt2,\begin{split}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!||F(U)||_{L_{x}^{2}L_{t}^{2}}&\leq C\sigma^{\alpha}\left|\left|\int_{*}|\widehat{U}(\xi_{1},\tau_{1})|\cdots|\widehat{U}(\xi_{k-1},\tau_{k-1})||\widehat{D_{x}^{\alpha}U}(\xi_{k},\tau_{k})||\widehat{D_{x}U}(\xi_{k+1},\tau_{k+1})|\right|\right|_{L_{\xi}^{2}L_{\tau}^{2}}\\ &=C\sigma^{\alpha}||w_{1}\cdots w_{k+1}||_{L_{x}^{2}L_{t}^{2}},\end{split} (4.18)

where w1^​(ξ,τ)=⋯=wk−1^​(ξ,τ)=|U^​(ξ,τ)|\widehat{w_{1}}(\xi,\,\tau)=\cdots=\widehat{w_{k-1}}(\xi,\,\tau)=|\widehat{U}(\xi,\tau)|, wk^​(ξ,τ)=|Dxα​U^​(ξ,τ)|\widehat{w_{k}}(\xi,\,\tau)=|\widehat{D_{x}^{\alpha}U}(\xi,\tau)| and wk+1^​(ξ,τ)=|Dx​U^​(ξ,τ)|\widehat{w_{k+1}}(\xi,\,\tau)=|\widehat{D_{x}U}(\xi,\tau)|.

By applying Lemma 2.6 it follows from (4.18) that

‖F⁡(U)‖Lx2​Lt2≤Cσα∏i=1k−3||wi||X12+,b||wk−2||X0,b⋯||wk+1||X0,b=C​σα​(∏i=1k−3‖U‖X12+,b)​‖U‖X0,b2​‖Dxα​U‖X0,b||Dx​U||X0,b≤C​σα​‖U‖X1,bk+1.\begin{split}||F(U)||_{L_{x}^{2}L_{t}^{2}}&\leq C{\sigma}^{\alpha}\prod_{i=1}^{k-3}||w_{i}||_{X^{\frac{1}{2}+,b}}||w_{k-2}||_{X^{0,b}}\cdots||w_{k+1}||_{X^{0,b}}\\ &=C{\sigma}^{\alpha}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k-3}||U||_{X^{\frac{1}{2}+,b}}\right)||U||^{2}_{X^{0,b}}||D_{x}^{\alpha}U||_{X^{0,b}}||D_{x}U||_{X^{0,b}}\\ &\leq C{\sigma}^{\alpha}||U||_{X^{1,b}}^{k+1}.\end{split}

This completes the proof of (4.11).

To prove (4.12), first observe that for 0≤j≤10\leq j\leq 1, one has ⟨ξ⟩−j≤|ξ|−j\langle\xi\rangle^{-j}\leq|\xi|^{-j} for all ξ≠0\xi\neq 0. Using this fact, we obtain

‖∂xF⁡(U)‖X0,b−1=‖⟨τ−ξ3⟩b−1​|ξ|​|F⁡(U)^​(ξ,τ)|‖Lξ2​Lτ2≤‖⟨τ−ξ3⟩b−1​⟨ξ⟩j​|ξ|1−j​|F⁡(U)^​(ξ,τ)|‖Lξ2​Lτ2.\begin{split}||\partial_{x}F(U)||_{X^{0,\,b-1}}&=||\langle\tau-\xi^{3}\rangle^{b-1}|\xi||\widehat{F(U)}(\xi,\tau)|||_{L_{\xi}^{2}L_{\tau}^{2}}\\ &\leq||\langle\tau-\xi^{3}\rangle^{b-1}\langle\xi\rangle^{j}|\xi|^{1-j}|\widehat{F(U)}(\xi,\tau)|||_{L_{\xi}^{2}L_{\tau}^{2}}.\end{split} (4.19)

Assuming |ξ1|≤⋯≤|ξk+1||\xi_{1}|\leq\cdots\leq|\xi_{k+1}|, one has |ξ|1−j≤(k+1)1−j​|ξk+1|1−j|\xi|^{1-j}\leq(k+1)^{1-j}|\xi_{k+1}|^{1-j} and using (4.16), the estimate (4.19) yields

‖∂xF⁡(U)‖X0,b−1≤C​σα​||⟨τ−ξ3⟩b−1​⟨ξ⟩j​|ξ|1−j​|ξ​|∫∗|ξk|α|​U^​(ξ1,τ1)​|⋯|​U^​(ξk+1,τk+1)|||Lξ2​Lτ2≤C​σα​||⟨τ−ξ3⟩b−1​⟨ξ⟩j​|ξ​|∫∗|ξk|α​|ξk+1|1−j|​U^​(ξ1,τ1)​|⋯|​U^​(ξk+1,τk+1)|||Lξ2​Lτ2=Cσα||∂x(v1⋯vk+1)||Xj,b−1,\begin{split}||\partial_{x}F(U)||_{X^{0,\,b-1}}&\leq C\sigma^{\alpha}\left|\left|\langle\tau-\xi^{3}\rangle^{b-1}\langle\xi\rangle^{j}|\xi|^{1-j}|\xi|\int_{*}|\xi_{k}|^{\alpha}|\widehat{U}(\xi_{1},\tau_{1})|\cdots|\widehat{U}(\xi_{k+1},\tau_{k+1})|\right|\right|_{L_{\xi}^{2}L_{\tau}^{2}}\\ &\leq C\sigma^{\alpha}\left|\left|\langle\tau-\xi^{3}\rangle^{b-1}\langle\xi\rangle^{j}|\xi|\int_{*}|\xi_{k}|^{\alpha}|\xi_{k+1}|^{1-j}|\widehat{U}(\xi_{1},\tau_{1})|\cdots|\widehat{U}(\xi_{k+1},\tau_{k+1})|\right|\right|_{L_{\xi}^{2}L_{\tau}^{2}}\\ &=C\sigma^{\alpha}||\partial_{x}(v_{1}\cdots v_{k+1})||_{X^{j,\,b-1}},\end{split} (4.20)

for v1,…,vk+1v_{1},...,v_{k+1} defined by v1^​(ξ,τ)=⋯=vk−1^​(ξ,τ)=|U^​(ξ,τ)|\widehat{v_{1}}(\xi,\,\tau)=\cdots=\widehat{v_{k-1}}(\xi,\,\tau)=|\widehat{U}(\xi,\tau)|, vk^​(ξ,τ)=|Dxα​U^​(ξ,τ)|\widehat{v_{k}}(\xi,\,\tau)=|\widehat{D_{x}^{\alpha}U}(\xi,\tau)| and vk+1^​(ξ,τ)=|Dx1−j​U^​(ξ,τ)|\widehat{v_{k+1}}(\xi,\,\tau)=|\widehat{D_{x}^{1-j}U}(\xi,\tau)|.

For every j>k−42​kj>\frac{k-4}{2k}, we can use the estimate (2.7) with b=12+ϵb=\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon, to obtain from (4.20) that

‖∂xF⁡(U)‖X0,b−1≤Cσα||v1||Xj,b⋯||vk+1||Xj,b=C​σα​(∏i=1k−1‖U‖Xj,b)​‖Dxα​U‖Xj,b||Dx1−j​U||Xj,b≤C​σα​(∏i=1k−1‖U‖X1,b)​‖U‖Xj+α,b||U||X1,b.\begin{split}||\partial_{x}F(U)||_{X^{0,\,b-1}}&\leq C\sigma^{\alpha}||v_{1}||_{X^{j,\,b}}\cdots||v_{k+1}||_{X^{j,\,b}}\\ &=C\sigma^{\alpha}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}||U||_{X^{j,\,b}}\right)||D_{x}^{\alpha}U||_{X^{j,\,b}}||D_{x}^{1-j}U||_{X^{j,\,b}}\\ &\leq C\sigma^{\alpha}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}||U||_{X^{1,\,b}}\right)||U||_{X^{j+\alpha,\,b}}||U||_{X^{1,\,b}}.\\ \end{split} (4.21)

Now, we choose j>k−42​kj>\frac{k-4}{2k} and α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] such that j+α≤1j+\alpha\leq 1. Indeed, for δ>0\delta>0 arbitrarialy small, considering j=k−42​k+δj=\frac{k-4}{2k}+\delta we get j+α≤1j+\alpha\leq 1 if we choose α≤k+42​k−δ\alpha\leq\frac{k+4}{2k}-\delta. Therefore, for 0<α≤k+42​k−δ0<\alpha\leq\frac{k+4}{2k}-\delta, from (4.21) one has

‖∂xF⁡(U)‖X0,b−1≤C​σα​‖U‖X1,bk+1,||\partial_{x}F(U)||_{X^{0,\,b-1}}\leq C\sigma^{\alpha}||U||_{X^{1,b}}^{k+1},

as desired. ∎

In the following we use the estimate obtained in Lemma 4.1 to prove that the quantity Eσ​(t)E_{\sigma}(t) defined in (4.1) is almost conserved.

Proposition 4.2.

Let σ>0\sigma>0 and α∈[0,k+42​k)\alpha\in[0,\,\frac{k+4}{2k}). Then for any b=12+ϵb=\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon, 0<ϵ≪10<\epsilon\ll 1, there exists C>0C>0 such that for any solution u∈XTσ, 1,bu\in X_{T}^{\sigma,\,1,\,b} to the IVP (1.1) in the interval [0,T][0,\,T], we have

supt∈[0,T]Eσ​(t)≤Eσ​(0)+C​σα​‖u‖XTσ, 1,bk+2​(1+‖u‖XTσ, 1,bk).\sup_{t\in[0,\,T]}E_{\sigma}(t)\leq E_{\sigma}(0)+C\sigma^{\alpha}||u||_{X_{T}^{\sigma,\,1,\,b}}^{k+2}(1+||u||_{X_{T}^{\sigma,\,1,\,b}}^{k}). (4.22)
Proof.

Recalling (4.9) and (4.10), we have to estimate each term of |Rσ​(t′)||R_{\sigma}(t^{\prime})| for all 0<t′≤T0<t^{\prime}\leq T. For the first and the third terms in (4.10) we use the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, Lemmas 2.2 and 2.4 and the estimate (4.11) restricted to the time slab and obtain that for any b=12+ϵb=\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon, 0<ϵ≪10<\epsilon\ll 1, there exists C>0C>0 such that

|∫∫⁡χ[0,t′]​U​F​(U)​dx​dt|≤‖χ[0,t′]​U‖Lx2​Lt2​‖χ[0,t′]​F​(U)‖Lx2​Lt2≤‖U‖XT0, 0||F⁡(U)||XT0, 0≤C​σα​‖u‖XTσ, 1,bk+2\begin{split}\left|\int\int\chi_{[0,\,t^{\prime}]}UF(U)dxdt\right|&\leq||\chi_{[0,\,t^{\prime}]}U||_{L_{x}^{2}L_{t}^{2}}||\chi_{[0,\,t^{\prime}]}F(U)||_{L_{x}^{2}L_{t}^{2}}\\ &\leq||U||_{X_{T}^{0,\,0}}||F(U)||_{X_{T}^{0,\,0}}\\ &\leq C\sigma^{\alpha}||u||_{X_{T}^{\sigma,\,1,\,b}}^{k+2}\end{split} (4.23)

and

|∫∫⁡χ[0,t′]​Uk+1​F​(U)​dx​dt|≤‖χ[0,t′]​Uk+1‖Lx2​Lt2​‖χ[0,t′]​F​(U)‖Lx2​Lt2≤‖Uk+1‖XT0, 0||F⁡(U)||XT0, 0≤C​σα​‖u‖XTσ, 1,b2​(k+1),\begin{split}\left|\int\int\chi_{[0,\,t^{\prime}]}U^{k+1}F(U)dxdt\right|&\leq||\chi_{[0,\,t^{\prime}]}U^{k+1}||_{L_{x}^{2}L_{t}^{2}}||\chi_{[0,\,t^{\prime}]}F(U)||_{L_{x}^{2}L_{t}^{2}}\\ &\leq||U^{k+1}||_{X_{T}^{0,\,0}}||F(U)||_{X_{T}^{0,\,0}}\\ &\leq C\sigma^{\alpha}||u||_{X_{T}^{\sigma,\,1,\,b}}^{2(k+1)},\end{split} (4.24)

for all 0<t′≤T0<t^{\prime}\leq T.

For the second term in (4.10), we use the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, Lemma 2.2 and estimate (4.12), to obtain

|∫∫χ[0,t′]​∂xU​∂x(F⁡(U))​dx​dt|≤‖χ[0,t′]​∂xU‖X0, 1−b||χ[0,t′]​∂x(F⁡(U))||X0,b−1≤‖∂xU‖XT0, 1−b||∂x(F⁡(U))||XT0,b−1≤C​σα​‖u‖XTσ, 1,bk+2,\begin{split}\left|\int\int\chi_{[0,\,t^{\prime}]}\partial_{x}U\partial_{x}(F(U))dxdt\right|&\leq||\chi_{[0,\,t^{\prime}]}\partial_{x}U||_{X^{0,\,1-b}}||\chi_{[0,\,t^{\prime}]}\partial_{x}(F(U))||_{X^{0,\,b-1}}\\ &\leq||\partial_{x}U||_{X_{T}^{0,\,1-b}}||\partial_{x}(F(U))||_{X_{T}^{0,\,b-1}}\\ &\leq C\sigma^{\alpha}||u||_{X_{T}^{\sigma,\,1,\,b}}^{k+2},\end{split} (4.25)

for all 0<t′≤T0<t^{\prime}\leq T, where 12<b<1\frac{1}{2}<b<1 is the same as before.

The result follows combining the estimates (4.23), (4.24) and (4.25). ∎

Corollary 4.3.

Let σ>0\sigma>0, kk even and α∈[0,k+22​k)\alpha\in[0,\frac{k+2}{2k}). Then there exists C>0C>0 such that the solution u∈XTσ, 1,bu\in X_{T}^{\sigma,\,1,\,b} to the IVP (1.1) in the defocusing case (μ=−1\mu=-1) given by Theorem 1.1, we have

supt∈[0,T]Eσ​(t)≤Eσ​(0)+C​σα​Eσ​(0)k2+1​(1+Eσ​(0)k2).\sup_{t\in[0,\,T]}E_{\sigma}(t)\leq E_{\sigma}(0)+C\sigma^{\alpha}E_{\sigma}(0)^{\frac{k}{2}+1}(1+E_{\sigma}(0)^{\frac{k}{2}}). (4.26)
Proof.

For μ=−1\mu=-1, from (4.1), since kk is even, we have

Eσ​(0)=‖u0‖Gσ, 12+2(k+1)​(k+2)​‖eσ​|Dx|​u0‖Lxk+2k+2≥||u0||Gσ, 12.E_{\sigma}(0)=||u_{0}||_{G^{\sigma,\,1}}^{2}+\frac{2}{(k+1)(k+2)}||e^{\sigma|D_{x}|}u_{0}||_{L^{k+2}_{x}}^{k+2}\geq||u_{0}||_{G^{\sigma,\,1}}^{2}. (4.27)

From (3.6) and (4.27), we get

‖u‖XTσ, 1,b≤C​Eσ​(0)12.||u||_{X_{T}^{\sigma,\,1,\,b}}\leq CE_{\sigma}(0)^{\frac{1}{2}}. (4.28)

The required estimate follows from (4.22) and the estimate (4.28). ∎

Remark 4.4.

For the solutions to the IVP (1.1) with kk odd we do not know the sign of ∫(eσ​|Dx|​u)k+2​𝑑x\int(e^{\sigma|D_{x}|}u)^{k+2}dx and it is not possible to have an inequality of the form (4.27).

For the solutions to the IVP (1.1) in the focusing case (μ=1\mu=1) with kk even, from (4.1), one has

Eσ​(0)=‖u0‖Gσ, 12−2(k+1)​(k+2)​‖eσ​|Dx|​u0‖Lxk+2k+2≤||u0||Gσ, 12,E_{\sigma}(0)=||u_{0}||_{G^{\sigma,\,1}}^{2}-\frac{2}{(k+1)(k+2)}||e^{\sigma|D_{x}|}u_{0}||_{L^{k+2}_{x}}^{k+2}\leq||u_{0}||_{G^{\sigma,\,1}}^{2}, (4.29)

This estimate cannot be used to obtain an estimate of the form (4.26) which plays a crucial role in the argument used to prove the Theorem 1.2.

For this reason, we considered only the defocusing case with kk even to obtain the decay rate of the radius of spatial analyticity to the gKdV equation (1.1).

5. Global Analytic Solution - Proof of Theorem 1.2

Now we are in position to provide the proof of the main result of this work.

Remark 5.1.

There are several works (see for example [15], [18], [23]) in which the authors consider the gKdV equation in the periodic setting and obtained the local well-posedness results for given real analytic initial data. Recently, Himonas et al. in [17] considered the dispersion generalized KdV equation in the periodic setting and constructed almost conserved quantity at the L2L^{2}-level of Sobolev regularity to obtain an algebraic lower bound for radius of spatial analyticity for the global solution emanating from the real analytic initial data. This motivates one to initiate a similar study for the gKdV equation (1.1) with k≥2k\geq 2 as well. However, as discussed in the previous section, in the periodic case too it would be necessary to construct almost conserved quantity at the higher lever of Sobolev regularity. The multilinear estimates in the periodic setting are more delicate and that requires a considerable piece of work. This will be one of the topics that we intend to address in future projects.
